summary: Defines a way to compute a hash of a JSON Web Key. It specifies which fields are included, how to put them in a canonical form, and how to turn the result into bytes to hash. The hash can be used to identify or select a key.

eli5.summary: A fingerprint is a short mark that identifies a person. This gives every digital key a short fingerprint too.

questions: how to compute a hash of a json web key
how to compute a jwk thumbprint
can i use a jwk thumbprint as a kid

subtitle: A recipe for turning a JSON Web Key into a short, repeatable hash that names the key.

tldr.problem: A JSON Web Key can be written in many ways and can carry extra optional members, so there was no agreed way to compute a hash that identifies the key itself.
tldr.mechanism: Keep only the required members of the key, write them as JSON with no whitespace and in lexicographic order, then hash the UTF-8 octets with a chosen hash function such as SHA-256.
tldr.outcome: The same key gives the same thumbprint no matter which optional members travel with it, so the base64url-encoded thumbprint can serve as a key ID ("kid").

facts.label: Hash input
facts.value: UTF-8 JSON of required members only

today: RFC 7638 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the JSON Web Key specification, RFC 7517.

sections.title: Why Hash a Key
sections.content:
RFC 7638 defines a method for computing a hash value (also called a digest) over a JSON Web Key (JWK). The RFC says what it must settle: which fields of the JWK go into the hash, how to build a canonical form of those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into bytes to hash.

The resulting value is called a JWK Thumbprint. It can identify or select the key it was computed from. The RFC's own example is using the base64url-encoded thumbprint as a kid (key ID) value.

The terminology comes from the JWK, JWS and JWA specifications (RFC 7517, RFC 7515 and RFC 7518).
sections.eli5: Imagine every key has a long, complicated description. This RFC says how to boil that description down into one short code, the same way every time.

sections.title: The Two-Step Computation
sections.content:
The thumbprint is computed in two steps.

  1. Build a JSON object that holds only the required members of the JWK. It has no whitespace or line breaks around any syntactic element, and its members are ordered lexicographically by the Unicode code points of the member names. This object is itself a legal JWK for the same key.
  2. Hash the octets of the UTF-8 representation of that object with a cryptographic hash function H. SHA-256 is given as an example of H.

The output is the JWK Thumbprint of the JWK with H. The RFC also notes that a key does not have to be in JWK format to get a thumbprint. It only needs a defined JWK representation, and the party computing the hash needs the key material.
sections.eli5: First you copy only the must-have parts of the key onto a clean page, in alphabetical order. Then you run that page through a machine that squishes it into a short code.

sections.title: A Worked Example with an RSA Key
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an RSA public key that has the members kty, n, e, alg and kid. Only kty, n and e are required for an RSA public key, so only those are used. In lexicographic order they are e, kty, n.

The intermediate JSON object therefore starts {"e":"AQAB","kty":"RSA","n":"... and the alg and kid members are left out. Hashing its UTF-8 octets with SHA-256 gives a 32-octet value. Its base64url encoding in the RFC is NzbLsXh8uDCcd-6MNwXF4W_7noWXFZAfHkxZsRGC9Xs.
sections.eli5: The example shows a key with extra labels stuck on it. Those labels are thrown away, the important bits are lined up in order, and out comes a short code you could use as a name tag.

sections.title: Which Members Are Used
sections.content:
Only the required members of a key's JWK representation count. The RFC lists them, in lexicographic order, for the key types known at the time:

  • Elliptic curve public key: crv, kty, x, y
  • RSA public key: e, kty, n
  • Symmetric key: k, kty

For key types defined later, the specification that defines them should be consulted to learn which members besides kty are required.

Optional members are left out on purpose, so that the thumbprint refers to a key rather than a key plus a set of attributes. Different applications may attach different optional members to the same key, and including them would give different hashes for the same key.

For a private key, the thumbprint is computed as for the corresponding public key. Both halves of a key pair therefore share one thumbprint, and application context decides which one is meant.
sections.eli5: Only the parts every key of that kind must have go into the code. Stickers and notes on the key do not count, so the same key always gets the same code.

sections.title: Ordering, Escaping and Hash Choice
sections.content:
Members are ordered by the Unicode code points of their names. Several rules keep the hash input predictable:

  • Characters in member names and values MUST be written without escaping. Thumbprints of JWKs that need escaped characters are not defined by this specification.
  • If a member value is itself a JSON object, its members MUST also be ordered lexicographically. The RFC says none are defined that do.
  • Integer numbers MUST be written without a fraction or exponent part, so 1.024e3 must be written 1024. Thumbprints of non-integer numbers are not defined.

The RFC does not fix the hash function. An application chooses it, and SHA-256 is described as a good default at the time of writing. Often only the key's creator needs to know which function was used, because consumers treat the kid as an opaque value. When several parties recompute and compare thumbprints, they must agree on the same function.

Practical warnings: platform sort functions can disagree on non-ASCII characters, and JSON.stringify() cannot be counted on to sort members. All defined JWK member names and values use printable ASCII, which avoids most of these problems.
sections.eli5: To get the same code everyone must write the key exactly the same way: same order, no fancy escapes, plain whole numbers. Even a tiny difference in how it is written would give a different code.

sections.title: Comparison with X.509 Digests
sections.content:
A JWK Thumbprint covers only the members needed to represent a key. The RFC therefore says it is more like a digest of an X.509 Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) value than a digest of a whole certificate, such as the x5t value defined for X.509 certificates.

A thumbprint is logically equivalent to a digest of the SPKI form of the key, but it is computed over a JSON representation instead of an ASN.1 one.
sections.eli5: It is like fingerprinting just the key, not the whole ID card the key came with.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The JSON and Unicode comparison considerations of JWS (RFC 7515) also apply. If implementations mishandle esoteric or escaped characters, they may fail to identify the intended key. The RFC judges the impact on public keys to be limited, since a public key's information is already public.

A hash of a symmetric key could leak information about the key, so its thumbprint should typically be hidden from parties that do not hold the key. The exception is when the hash function is known to give enough protection.

A thumbprint identifies a key uniquely only if one unambiguous JWK representation exists and is used. For example, writing an RSA exponent as "AAEAAQ" instead of the correct "AQAB" would produce a different thumbprint for effectively the same key, unless the implementation validates the encoding.

Thumbprints are not a reliable way to blacklist keys. An attacker can supply a transformed key, such as an RSA key with modulus 3*N, that still works about 1/3 of the time but appears to be a different key.
sections.eli5: A code is a good name tag for a good key, but a sneaky person can make a slightly changed copy with a different code. So do not rely on codes alone to ban a key.

sections.title: IANA Registry Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC adds instructions for the Designated Experts of three registries in the JOSE registry group: JSON Web Key Types, JSON Web Key Elliptic Curve and JSON Web Key Parameters. IANA also added a link to this specification in their reference sections.

Because of the Unicode concerns above, the experts must either require that registered names and values use only printable ASCII, excluding the double quote and the backslash, or require that definitions using other code points specify the exact code point sequences. Registrations that can only be written with escaped characters must not be accepted.
sections.eli5: The people who keep the official list of key types are told to allow only plain, simple characters so that everybody can write the key the same way.
